Ductal adenocarcinoma is typically hypodense relative to healthy pancreas, especially in the pancreatic phase (about 40-45 seconds), when normal parenchyma enhances the most. About 10% are isodense: indirect signs (dilatation of the pancreatic duct or bile duct, "double duct" sign, upstream atrophy, contour deformity) should prompt a search for the mass.
A tumor of the head obstructs the common bile duct: dilated bile duct and distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign).
The report must state whether the tumor is resectable, describing the degree of contact for each vessel: superior mesenteric vein and portal vein (≤ 180° without irregularity = resectable; beyond that, or with irregularity/thrombosis = borderline), superior mesenteric artery, celiac trunk and hepatic artery (arterial contact over 180° = locally advanced). Arterial variants, lymph nodes, liver and peritoneum are also needed.
Differential diagnosis: focal or autoimmune pancreatitis, neuroendocrine tumor (hypervascular), metastasis, lymphoma.
Massa ipodensa in fase pancreatica + via: Hypodense mass in the pancreatic phase + dilated bile duct: adenocarcinoma; the report ends with vascular relationships in degrees.
Carcinoma duttale infiltrante del pancre: Infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the pancreas, pT3 pN1 M0 (AJCC stage IIB) on examination of the surgical specimen (CPTAC clinical data from the CPTAC-PDA collection).
